L18@P1: AI on the Edge: An Automated Pipeline for
L19@P1: PyTorch-to-Android Deployment and Benchmarking
L20@P1: Saif U Din *, Muhammad Ahsan Hussain, Mohsin Ikram, Faraz Kayani, Dmitry Ignatov
L21@P1: and Radu Timofte
L22@P1: Computer Vision Lab, CAIDAS & IFI, University of Würzburg, Germany
L23@P1: * Correspondence: saif.saif-u-din@uni-wuerzburg.de
L24@P1: Abstract
L25@P1: On-device latency ultimately determines whether a vision model is deployable on smartphones, yet
L26@P1: collecting real-device latency at scale is costly and fragile. We present AI on the Edge, an automated
L27@P1: measurement pipeline and open dataset for large-scale delegate-resolved Android benchmarking. AI
L28@P1: on the Edge converts a PyTorch model zoo to TensorFlow Lite in FP32 and full-integer INT8 precision,
L29@P1: then benchmarks each model on physical phones with three forced execution paths: CPU (XNNPACK),
L30@P1: GPU (TFLite GPU), and NPU (NNAPI), so every latency is attributable to a known backend. Using one workstation and five commodity phones, AI on the Edge measured 586 architectures and
L31@P1: produced 5,826 model × device × precision records, comprising about 17 500 backend benchmarks
L32@P1: and 351 600 timed inferences (586 × 5 × 3 × 2 × 20), in roughly 56 unattended device-hours (up to
L33@P1: 201 models/h/phone). Campaigns include both end-to-end Stage A+Stage B runs and Stage B-only
L34@P1: replay from prebuilt TFLite artifacts, with identical on-device benchmark settings. The pipeline is
L35@P1: designed for unattended operation via USB-reconnection handling, thermal cool-down scheduling,
L36@P1: and a resumable processing ledger. We release the full per-run dataset with documented schema,
L37@P1: public model/code resources, and a reproducibility harness that regenerates headline statistics from
L38@P1: raw records. AI on the Edge reduces the practical cost of real-device benchmarking and provides a
L39@P1: reusable substrate for hardware-aware architecture research.
L40@P1: Keywords: mobile AI benchmarking; on-device inference; TensorFlow Lite; delegate-aware measurement; open dataset
L41@P1: 1. Introduction
L42@P1: Mobile inference latency is the quantity that decides whether a vision model ships. Despite this,
L43@P1: the efficient-vision community still optimises and reports proxies most commonly FLOPs or parameter
L44@P1: counts [1] because measuring latency on real hardware at the scale of a model-search campaign is
L45@P1: laborious and brittle. The dominant alternatives both trade away fidelity or coverage. Hardware
L46@P1: latency predictors such as nn-Meter [2] and BRP-NAS [3] avoid the device after an initial profiling
L47@P1: phase, but they estimate latency and cannot expose the runtime-stack effects (delegate fallback, DVFS,
L48@P1: memory-bandwidth limits) that govern real deployments. Curated real-hardware suites such as
L49@P1: MLPerf Mobile [4] and the AI-Benchmark/LETI line [5] run on physical phones but cover only a
L50@P1: handful of fixed reference networks, which is insufficient for architecture search or for studying how a
L51@P1: population of architectures behaves across hardware. This gap is particularly relevant across the spectrum of architectures that now target deployment: from classic backbones such as ResNet [6] trained
L52@P1: on large-scale recognition benchmarks [7], through efficient-vision families such as MobileNets [8–10],
L53@P1: ShuffleNet [1,11], SqueezeNet [12], and EfficientNet [13], to mobile vision transformers [14,15] and
L54@P1: recent deployment-oriented designs like MobileOne [16], where paper-level complexity metrics often
L55@P1: diverge from observed on-device latency.

L61@P2: The practical obstacle is engineering, not science. Driving a phone over adb for thousands of
L62@P2: measurements surfaces a long tail of failure modes: USB resets, thermal throttling that silently corrupts
L63@P2: timings, delegates that fall back to CPU without warning, and per-model conversion errors that abort
L64@P2: an unattended run. A benchmark that cannot survive these conditions cannot scale.
L65@P2: This paper contributes the infrastructure and the resource, not a new scientific claim about any
L66@P2: particular architecture. Concretely:
L67@P2: • An automated, fault-tolerant pipeline (AI on the Edge). A two-stage system that (i) converts an
L68@P2: arbitrary PyTorch zoo to TFLite in FP32 and full-integer INT8 precision with host-side accuracy
L69@P2: evaluation, and (ii) benchmarks every model on physical phones with three forced delegates,
L70@P2: recovering automatically from USB loss, thermal events, and conversion failures (Section 3).
L71@P2: • A delegate-resolved measurement protocol. For every model × device × precision we record
L72@P2: CPU, GPU, and NPU latency separately plus a winner label, so each number is attributable to a
L73@P2: known execution path rather than an opaque default invocation (Section 3.2).
L74@P2: • An open dataset and throughput characterisation. 5,826 records over 586 topologies and five
L75@P2: SoCs, collected in ≈56 unattended device-hours at up to 201 models/h/phone, released with a
L76@P2: documented schema and reproducibility harness (Sections 4–5).
L77@P2: AI on the Edge is deliberately scoped as a measurement and data contribution; the statistical
L78@P2: interpretation of the resulting dataset (e.g. complexity–latency modelling) is the subject of a separate
L79@P2: study and is out of scope here. For readability, the paper follows the pipeline order: Section 3
L80@P2: describes conversion (including Stage A accuracy retention) and device benchmarking; Sections 4 and
L81@P2: 5 present what was collected and at what cost; Section 6 reports dataset-quality diagnostics; Section 7
L82@P2: demonstrates immediate queryability; and Sections 8–10 cover release logistics, limitations, and final
L83@P2: takeaways.
L84@P2: 2. Related Work
L85@P2: Latency Predictors.
L86@P2: nn-Meter [2] predicts per-model inference latency by decomposing graphs into hardware-aware
L87@P2: kernels; BRP-NAS [3] trains a GCN latency predictor for NAS. Both require an initial on-device
L88@P2: profiling corpus and then infer latency. AI on the Edge is complementary: it produces exactly the kind
L89@P2: of broad, real measurement corpus such predictors must be trained and validated against, but with
L90@P2: explicit per-delegate attribution.
L91@P2: Real-Hardware Suites.
L92@P2: MLPerf Mobile [4] standardises a small set of reference tasks for cross-vendor comparison; AIBenchmark/LETI [5] ranks devices on a fixed workload and MLPerf Tiny [17] extends standardised
L93@P2: benchmarking to microcontroller-class hardware — again on a small fixed task set. These prioritise
L94@P2: device comparison on few models, whereas AI on the Edge prioritises architecture-population coverage
L95@P2: on commodity phones.
L96@P2: Architecture-Population Studies.
L97@P2: Li et al. [18] benchmark 102 CNNs and 69 ViTs across six mobile platforms, the closest prior
L98@P2: effort in spirit. AI on the Edge differs by (i) automating the full PyTorch→TFLite →device path for a
L99@P2: larger, non-curated zoo, (ii) forcing and recording all three delegates per model, and (iii) releasing the
L100@P2: complete per-run dataset with a reproducibility harness. An earlier preprint from our group focused
L101@P2: on an automated deployment and benchmarking pipeline [? ]; the present manuscript is the improved
L102@P2: real-physical-mobile-device resource paper with expanded dataset accounting, quality diagnostics,
L103@P2: and release packaging. At the model level, MobileOne [16] further highlights that practical latency
L104@P2: ranking can disagree with nominal complexity even for architectures explicitly designed for mobile
L105@P2: deployment.

L108@P3: Hardware-Aware NAS and Quantization.
L109@P3: MnasNet [19], FBNet [20], and ProxylessNAS [21] fold measured latency into search, and resourceconstrained variants such as MCUNet [22] push this to microcontroller budgets; post-training and
L110@P3: quantization-aware methods study the accuracy cost of INT8 [23,24], while complementary compression techniques pruning/quantization codesign [25] and knowledge distillation [26] further reshape
L111@P3: the deployable model population. These consume on-device measurements as an input; AI on the
L112@P3: Edge is the tool that makes such measurements cheap to obtain at scale. From a systems perspective,
L113@P3: the roofline model [27] remains a useful lens for interpreting why runtime behavior can shift across
L114@P3: CPU/GPU/NPU paths despite similar FLOPs budgets.
L115@P3: 3. System Design
L116@P3: AI on the Edge is a two-stage pipeline (Figure 1). Stage A runs on a workstation and turns a model
L117@P3: zoo into deployable TFLite binaries with host-side accuracy labels. Stage B drives physical phones
L118@P3: over adb and records delegate-resolved latency. The stages are decoupled through the filesystem and a
L119@P3: job ledger, so either can be re-run independently.

L144@P3: Figure 1. AI on the Edge pipeline. Stage A (top) converts a PyTorch zoo to FP32 TFLite and INT8 TFLite (generated
L145@P3: via PTQ) with host-side accuracy labels; Stage B (bottom) benchmarks each binary on physical phones under three
L146@P3: forced delegates and records a winner-resolved JSON. A guardian process makes the unattended run robust to
L147@P3: USB loss, thermal throttling, and conversion failures.
L148@P3: 3.1. Stage A: Conversion and Accuracy Labelling
L149@P3: For each architecture, AI on the Edge loads the epoch-50 checkpoint, infers the native input
L150@P3: resolution from the model’s preprocessing transform, and converts to TFLite via ai_edge_torch.
L151@P3: Two binaries are produced: a default FP32 export and a full-integer INT8 export using post-training
L152@P3: quantization (per-channel symmetric weights and activations) calibrated on 50 training images. We use
L153@P3: a fixed epoch-50 snapshot for every model because this is the uniform checkpoint available for the full
L154@P3: released zoo; using one common epoch keeps conversion and benchmarking inputs consistent across
L155@P3: architectures and devices. Top-1 accuracy for both precisions is evaluated host-side on CIFAR-10 [28]
L156@P3: in an isolated subprocess so that a single faulty model cannot crash the batch. The resulting binaries
L157@P3: and accuracy labels are the inputs to Stage B and are also published as a model zoo.
L158@P3: To keep the pipeline narrative linear, we report the Stage A quantization quality diagnostic here
L159@P3: (rather than later in the paper). Beyond rank-agreement, we characterise how much accuracy the
L160@P3: full-integer path costs across the entire released zoo (host-side CIFAR-10 top-1, n=586 models; Table 1).
L161@P3: The median absolute top-1 change from FP32 to INT8 is only 0.1 percentage points (pp) and the mean is
L162@P3: 1.6 pp PTQ is effectively lossless for the typical model. Restricting to the 563 models with a non-trivial
L163@P3: FP32 baseline (≥0.20), 95.9% stay within 2 pp of their FP32 accuracy; only 11 models lose more than
L164@P3: half their accuracy and 7 collapse to near-zero. These tail cases are deliberately retained in the zoo
L165@P3: with both precisions, so downstream users can study them rather than have them silently filtered.

L180@P4: 3.2. Stage B: Delegate-Resolved On-Device Benchmarking
L181@P4: Each TFLite binary is pushed to the phone and timed with the official TFLite benchmark_model
L182@P4: binary under three forced configurations: CPU-only (XNNPACK, GPU/NNAPI disabled), GPUonly (TFLite GPU delegate), and NPU-only (NNAPI). Concretely, each configuration invokes
L183@P4: benchmark_model –graph=<m> –num_runs=20 with the matching delegate flag (–use_xnnpack=true
L184@P4: –use_gpu=false –use _nnapi=false for CPU, –use_gpu=true –use_nnapi=false for GPU, and
L185@P4: –use_nnapi=true –use_gpu= false for NPU). We fix –num_runs=20 and leave warm-up at the tool
L186@P4: default (we do not pass –warmup_runs explicitly). Because default warm-up behavior can vary across
L187@P4: TFLite/LiteRT versions, we pin the benchmark_model binary version (Table 2) and interpret reported
L188@P4: mean/min/max/std exactly as emitted by that binary, i.e. over timed runs after internal warmup/initialisation. This amortises one-time delegate initialisation and graph compilation, so transient
L189@P4: first-run costs do not inflate the recorded latency. We define the primary latency as the minimum of
L190@P4: the valid per-delegate medians and store the corresponding winning backend (CPU, GPU, or NPU) as
L191@P4: a categorical label. Forcing the delegate rather than trusting an opaque default invocation is what
L192@P4: makes each measurement attributable to a specific execution path and is the methodological core
L193@P4: of the dataset. All benchmarking campaigns are executed on one device at a time over ADB (single
L194@P4: active target), and the full model sweep is then repeated independently on each phone. We do not run
L195@P4: cross-device parallel benchmarking in a shared session.
L196@P4: Campaign Modes (End-to-End vs Benchmark-Only).
L197@P4: The benchmark protocol is identical across runs, but two operational modes are used in practice:
L198@P4: (i) end-to-end Stage A+Stage B (convert/quantize on host, then benchmark on device) and (ii) Stage Bonly replay (download prebuilt TFLite artifacts from the released model zoo and benchmark directly).
L199@P4: No retraining is performed in either mode. This distinction changes wall-clock campaign time but not
L200@P4: per-model runtime measurement semantics: the same benchmark_model command, delegates, run count,
L201@P4: warm-up handling, parser, and JSON schema are used in both modes.
L202@P4: 3.3. Robustness for Unattended Operation
L203@P4: Three mechanisms allow AI on the Edge to run for many hours without supervision:
L204@P4: • Reconnection guardian. Every adb call is wrapped; on “device not found”/“device lost” the run
L205@P4: blocks, polls adb get-state, re-enables stay-awake, and resumes at the same model. USB resets
L206@P4: therefore cost time, not data.
L207@P4: • Thermal management. A short cool-down separates models and a longer cool-down plus a full
L208@P4: process restart is triggered every N=50 models, bounding die temperature so that timings are not
L209@P4: silently inflated by throttling.
L210@P4: • Resumable ledger and error capture. A JSON ledger records processed and failed model IDs;
L211@P4: restarts skip completed work. Benchmark stderr is scanned for delegate/compilation errors,
L212@P4: which are extracted to a per-device log with full raw output for auditing.

L215@P5: A model whose INT8 conversion fails still contributes its FP32 measurements; a model whose every delegate fails is recorded with valid=false and per-backend error strings rather than being
L216@P5: dropped silently. Each device run writes device-specific JSON outputs (android_<device>.json) and
L217@P5: corresponding error logs, enabling independent replay and audit of every device campaign.
L218@P5: 3.4. Implementation and Toolchain
L219@P5: Stage A converts PyTorch [29] models to TFLite and applies post-training quantization through
L220@P5: ai_edge_torch; Stage B drives every device with the official TFLite/LiteRT [30] benchmark_model
L221@P5: binary over adb. To make the conversion and measurement path reproducible, Table 2 pins the exact
L222@P5: toolchain used to collect the released dataset.

L235@P5: 4. The AI on the Edge Dataset
L236@P5: 4.1. Model Zoo and Devices
L237@P5: The zoo comprises 586 structurally diverse topologies — residual and depthwise-separable CNNs,
L238@P5: attention models, lightweight NAS-derived designs, and manually authored blocks retained by a
L239@P5: deliberately non-selective survival filter: any model that converts is kept, so the population reflects real
L240@P5: Android-deployable architectures rather than a hand-picked mobile-friendly subset. Measurements
L241@P5: span five commodity phones covering three SoC vendors and the full market tier (Table 3).

L252@P5: 4.2. Record Schema
L253@P5: Each record is one model × device × precision observation. The fields group into identity, validity,
L254@P5: latency, and device telemetry (Table 4). Per-backend min/max/std support uncertainty-aware analysis,
L255@P5: and the embedded device analytics (CPU core layout, ISA features, SoC string, live memory) make
L256@P5: every record self-describing and auditable.

L271@P6: 5. Throughput and Cost
L272@P6: We characterise AI on the Edge by the metric that motivates it: how cheaply it turns a zoo into real
L273@P6: measurements. Wall-clock spans are taken from the timestamps embedded in each record and therefore
L274@P6: include conversion, all six benchmark sessions per model (3 delegates × 2 precisions), parsing, and
L275@P6: the deliberate thermal cool-downs.
L276@P6: Interpretation Note for Campaign-Time Comparisons.
L277@P6: Because the project includes both end-to-end (Stage A+Stage B) campaigns and Stage B-only replay
L278@P6: campaigns from downloaded TFLite binaries, wall-clock throughput is mode-dependent. Stage B-only
L279@P6: runs remove conversion/quantization overhead and are therefore expected to complete faster even
L280@P6: with identical on-device benchmarking settings. To avoid reviewer ambiguity, we interpret campaigntime numbers as operational throughput under the executed mode, while hardware/runtime comparisons
L281@P6: should rely on per-record delegate latencies (cpu/gpu/npu_duration) that are mode-invariant.
L282@P6: A fixed thermal budget is built into every run by design and is independent of SoC speed: a
L283@P6: 2 s pause separates consecutive models, and a 60 s cool-down followed by a full process restart is
L284@P6: triggered every 50 models. This amounts to roughly 3 s of mandatory cool-down per model regardless
L285@P6: of how fast the phone computes. On the fastest handsets this fixed budget is a large fraction of
L286@P6: per-model wall-clock, which is why throughput saturates near 200 models/h rather than scaling with
L287@P6: raw compute; on the entry-tier MediaTek device, additional throttling-driven slow-downs dominate
L288@P6: instead. Table 5 reports the per-device wall-clock and throughput for the full sweep, and Figure 2
L289@P6: visualises the same per-device throughput.
